Plate-format PDMS microfluidic culture devices from hybrid SU-8/3D-printed resin wafer
molds
Tristan Simas1,#, Yonatan Morocz2, Jathav Puvirajan1, David Juncker2, and Alyson Fournier1
1Department of Neurology and Neurosurgery, Montréal Neurological Institute, McGill University,
Montréal, Québec, Canada 
2Victor Phillip Dahdaleh Institute of Genomic Medicine, McGill University, Montréal, QC,
Canada.
#Corresponding author

2
Abstract
Multi-well microfluidic culture platforms combine micrometer-scale channels with millimeter-
scale reservoirs, but their fabrication often requires labor-intensive alignment and individual well
punching. Here, we present OpenMFD, an open-source design and fabrication workflow for
producing reusable hybrid molds for plate-format microfluidic devices. Parametric design tools
generate matched photomasks and three-dimensional (3D) printable insert arrays from shared
device dimensions. The molds combine SU-8 photolithography for fine channel features with well-
forming inserts produced using a consumer resin 3D printer. Matching alignment pins and holes
enable the entire insert array to be aligned with and bonded to the patterned wafer in a single
operation. We fabricated polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) plates containing 48 two-compartment
devices with 96 wells on a standard 9 mm grid, forming all well openings during casting without
individual punching. Three reusable molds collectively produced more than 50 usable casts. The
assembled plates supported multichannel pipetting and automated imaging on high-content
microscopy systems without instrument modification. Primary cortical neurons were maintained
for 11 days in vitro, and distal tracer application produced retrograde labeling of neuronal cell
bodies, supporting axonal access to the distal compartment. This workflow coordinates device
design and mold assembly to support customizable, repeated production of compartmentalized
microfluidic culture plates.
Introduction
Compartmentalized microfluidic cultures permit independent access to neuronal cell bodies and
axons, enabling localized perturbations, axonal sampling, and studies of injury, regeneration and
transport (PMID: 16094385). Subsequent designs have supported controlled axon-guidance
gradients (PMID: 26000554), localized neuron–glia interactions (PMID: 22828584), and
customizable neuronal networks (PMID: 35466333). Microchannel geometry also influences the
performance of cultures connecting neuronal populations (PMID: 36111641). These capabilities
make compartmentalized devices valuable for investigating neuronal responses to spatially defined
signals, particularly when multiple experimental conditions must be compared in parallel. Related
compartmentalized systems have also enabled analysis of localized GDNF-dependent axon
entrapment (PMID: 30081039).
Parallel neuronal microfluidic assays are already established. A plate-compatible platform with up
to 96 independently addressable, three-compartment culture units has supported primary rodent
and human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived neurons (PMID: 38150531). A 40-unit
microtiter-format device has supported three-dimensional motor-axon outgrowth studies (PMID:
33483540). Modular microfluidic units offer reconfigurable neuronal culture arrangements
(PMID: 35466333), whereas fluid-walled circuits permit human neuronal culture and moderate-
throughput axotomy assays (PMID: 38841815). Together, these studies establish the feasibility of
parallel neuronal assays while illustrating how device architectures and fabrication workflows can
vary. Adapting and reproducing such platforms for specific experimental needs remains an
important practical consideration.
A persistent manufacturing challenge is the integration of micrometer-scale channels with
millimeter-scale, pipette-accessible culture reservoirs. Conventional polydimethylsiloxane
(PDMS) soft lithography readily replicates lithographically patterned microfeatures, but reservoirs
are commonly opened individually after curing, increasing manual handling as device numbers

3
grow. For compartmentalized neuronal cultures, microchannel dimensions must also remain
suitable for selective neurite access and robust experimental performance (PMID: 36111641).
Multiscale molding has addressed this mismatch: hybrid milled and hot-embossed masters enabled
simultaneous replication of channels and larger reservoirs without punching (PMID: 20049640),
including in neuron–glia co-culture devices (PMID: 22828584). Hybrid additive manufacturing
has also combined photolithographic channel features with printed compartment structures to
avoid manual post-processing (PMID: 32832365). Other microfluidic manufacturing strategies
include CO2 laser-cut PDMS channels (DOI: 10.1109/COASE.2007.4341853) and rapidly
fabricated optical-adhesive culture chips (PMID: 26657733). Micro-to-millimeter fabrication by
combining 3D printing and photolithography has also been reported (DOI:
10.7567/1347-4065/ab09d0). The fabrication approaches are compared in Supplementary Table
S1. Thus, multiscale fabrication and the elimination of reservoir punching are established; an
important remaining objective is to coordinate customizable plate-scale geometries with efficient,
repeatable mold assembly.
Photolithography offers reliable definition of fine channels, whereas resin-based three-dimensional
(3D) printing is well suited to larger structures and rapid changes in geometry. Directly printed
resin molds can nevertheless require post-treatment to mitigate PDMS curing inhibition and
facilitate release (PMID: 40190179). Hybrid soft-lithography and printed-component systems
provide other routes to tailored microfluidic devices (PMID: 40667579). Related combinations of
photolithography and additive manufacturing have also been applied to electrode fabrication (DOI:
10.1016/j.mne.2022.100124). Parylene C has been shown to protect resin-printed components in
primary-cell applications (PMID: 37534979). A related neuron–oligodendrocyte co-culture
platform integrated individually aligned 3D-printed metal inserts with SU-8 microfeatures (DOI:
10.1088/1361-6439/ab16a7). This precedent motivates an array-scale approach that coordinates
the design, positioning and attachment of many inserts in a single operation rather than repeating
insert alignment at individual locations.
Here, we introduce OpenMFD, an open-source parametric design and fabrication workflow for
reusable silicon-wafer molds that integrate photolithographically defined SU-8/SUEX structures
with resin-printed well-forming inserts. Shared design parameters generate matched photomasks,
insert arrays and plate-frame components, while corresponding pins and alignment openings
enable simultaneous transfer and bonding of the inserts to the wafer (Fig. 1). The retained inserts
form all reservoirs during subsequent PDMS casts, separating specialized mold fabrication from
routine device production. As a demonstration, we fabricated plates containing 48 two-
compartment neuronal devices and 96 wells on a standard 9 mm grid. We evaluated repeated
casting, multichannel pipetting, automated microscopy, directional tracer redistribution and
primary cortical neuron culture with retrograde axonal labeling. OpenMFD also generated
matched files for alternative compartment geometries. Additional software-generated
configurations are illustrated in Fig. 2; these alternatives were not fabricated or biologically tested.
Materials and Methods
Parametric design and fabrication-file generation - Microfluidic devices were designed using
OpenMFD (https://github.com/trissim/OpenMFD), an open-source parametric framework that
generates coordinated photolithographic masks, three-dimensional (3D) printable resin inserts, and
supporting plate components from shared design parameters. Device geometries were defined

4
using SolidPython and OpenSCAD. Two-dimensional photomasks were exported in Drawing
Exchange Format (DXF), while inserts and plate frames were exported as stereolithography (STL)
models. Matching coordinates defined the relative positions of the photolithographic features and
resin-insert alignment structures (Fig. 1).
The principal device comprised a 6 × 8 array of 48 two-compartment microfluidic units containing
96 wells on a standard 9 mm grid. Each device incorporated 62 microchannels with a nominal
width of 10 µm and 30 µm interchannel gaps. A horizontal scaling factor of 1.0226 was applied to
matching fabrication files to compensate for polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) shrinkage during
curing at 100 °C. Additional designs were generated for oligodendrocyte myelination, orthogonal-
gradient axon guidance, and three-compartment neuronal culture configurations. Design
dimensions are provided in Supplementary Data File 1, sheet S6, and alternative design geometries
are summarized in Fig. 2 and the OpenMFD repository.
Hybrid mold fabrication - Reusable hybrid molds were fabricated on 6-inch silicon wafers
by combining photolithographically patterned SU-8 and SUEX photoresists with 3D-printed
resin inserts (Fig. 3). The photolithographic structures comprised two nominally 5 µm layers
of SU-8 2005 (Kayaku Advanced Materials) and a 200 µm layer of SUEX K200 dry-film
photoresist (DJ MicroLaminates). The first SU-8 layer was uniformly exposed to form a
continuous base beneath the microchannel features. A second SU-8 layer was patterned
through the microchannel photomask, developed, and baked at 150 °C for 10 min before
SUEX lamination. The SUEX layer defined the well bases and alignment openings and was
exposed through an LP360 long-pass filter. Process-development observations are shown in
Supplementary Figs. S1–S2. Complete photolithographic processing parameters are
provided in Supplementary Protocol 1.
Well-forming inserts were produced from Siraya Tech Sculpt Clear resin using an Elegoo Mars 3
Pro resin printer (resin specifications: https://siraya.tech/products/sculpt-resin-high-temperature-
resistant-resin; printing settings: Supplementary Data File 1, sheet S2). The inserts were printed in
a coordinated array and retained on a detachable, flexible metal build plate for transfer to the
patterned wafer. Each insert contained a 1.85 × 1.85 mm alignment pin corresponding to a 2.0 ×
2.0 mm SUEX opening, providing a nominal clearance of 75 µm per side. EPO-TEK 301-2 epoxy
adhesive
 
(manufacturer
 
specifications:
https://products.meridianadhesives.com/storage/downloads/uennuicaaxt1bodtipkbpydtg0u8qs33/
301-2.pdf) was applied around the alignment pins, and the complete array was positioned against
the wafer. A compressible ethylene propylene diene monomer (EPDM) rubber backing was
incorporated into the clamping assembly. Following adhesive curing, the metal build plate was
flexed to release the bonded inserts. The completed mold received a conformal 1 µm parylene C
coating using an SCS 200 coating system. Detailed printing, alignment, bonding, washing, curing,
and coating procedures are provided in Supplementary Protocol 1.
PDMS casting and plate assembly - PDMS (Sylgard 184) was mixed at a 10:1 base-to-curing-
agent ratio and poured over the hybrid mold to a level below the tops of the well-forming inserts.
Approximately 30 mL was used per wafer. Filled molds were degassed under vacuum and cured
at 100 °C for 1 h. The cured PDMS arrays were demolded and trimmed to 108 × 72 mm along
molded cutting guides (Fig. 4).
The arrays were plasma-bonded to 110 × 74 × 0.17 mm glass sheets and sterilized by autoclaving.
Supporting plate frames were fabricated from high-impact polystyrene (HIPS) using a Creality

5
K1C filament printer (Supplementary Data File 1, sheet S3). The glass-bonded arrays were secured
within the frames using LOCTITE SI 5140 silicone adhesive (manufacturer specifications:
https://datasheets.tdx.henkel.com/LOCTITE-SI-5140-en_GL.pdf), cured at room temperature. A
second dry-air plasma treatment was performed before aqueous coating and cell culture. Detailed
casting, bonding, sterilization, frame assembly, and surface-treatment procedures are provided in
Supplementary Protocol 2.
Mold and device characterization - Printed insert-height variation was characterized by
measuring all 96 alignment pins in one array using a micrometer. Mold integrity was assessed by
inspecting the attachment of the photolithographic features and resin inserts. PDMS casts were
inspected for open wells, intact microchannels, and visible fabrication defects. Mold fabrication
and repeated casting were documented according to the acceptance criteria described in the
supplementary information. The individual 96 pin-height measurements are provided in
Supplementary Data File 1, sheet S1.
Apparent microchannel widths were estimated from brightfield images acquired from one interior
device on each of three independently assembled plates. Three transverse measurements were
obtained per device, using the centers of opposing dark channel-wall bands to define the measured
span. Measurements were calibrated using the image acquisition scale of 1.18675253 µm per pixel
(Supplementary Fig. S3; Supplementary Data File 1, sheet S4).
Compatibility with conventional liquid handling was evaluated using a multichannel pipette to fill
eight wells simultaneously. Automated imaging compatibility was assessed using Opera Phenix
Plus and ImageXpress Micro Confocal systems without modification to their plate-handling
hardware.
Fluorescent tracer transport assay - Directional tracer redistribution was examined in 24
two-compartment devices. Alexa Fluor 568-conjugated secondary antibody (1:1000 in
phosphate-buffered saline [PBS]) was introduced into the left compartment at 25 µL, while
Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated secondary antibody (1:1000 in PBS) was introduced into the
right compartment at 50 µL. Devices were imaged immediately after loading and following
72 h of incubation without replenishment or volume adjustment. Red and green fluorescence
distributions were compared qualitatively between the two time points (Fig. 5A).
Primary cortical neuron culture and retrograde axonal labeling - All rat experiments were
performed according to the guidelines set by the Canadian Council on Animal Care (CCAC), as
approved and overseen by the Neuro Animal Care Committee (Montreal Neurological Institute)
and the McGill Animal Compliance Office (ProtocolFournier-4748). Primary cortical neurons
were isolated from one embryonic day 18 Sprague Dawley rat embryo using an established
protocol (PMID: 18989412) and distributed across three independently assembled plates. The
plates therefore represented technical replicates of one neuronal preparation.
Culture wells were coated with dendritic polyglycerol amine (dPGA; DendroTEK Biosciences) at
10 µg/mL for 10 min (PMID: 35023760). Neurons were seeded into the somatic compartments at
5,000–10,000 cells per well in Dulbecco's modified Eagle medium containing 10% fetal bovine
serum. Following attachment, cultures were maintained in supplemented Neurobasal Plus
medium. Medium volumes of 50 µL in the somatic compartments and 25 µL in the distal
compartments established an initial hydrostatic volume difference. Cultures were maintained for
11 days in vitro (DIV).

6
At DIV10, cholera toxin subunit B conjugated to Alexa Fluor 647 (CTB-647) was applied to the
distal compartments at 1 µg/mL. Retrogradely labeled neuronal cell bodies were imaged 24 h later
at DIV11. One CTB-positive cell-body count was obtained per analyzed device. Analysis was
restricted to the 24 interior devices on each plate. Counts affected by image-segmentation artifacts
were excluded from quantitative summaries; cell-count magnitude alone was not an exclusion
criterion. All 72 device-level measurements, including the five artifact exclusion flags, are
provided in Supplementary Data File 1, sheet S5.
Imaging and data analysis - Fluorescence imaging was performed in widefield mode using a
PerkinElmer Opera Phenix Plus equipped with a 10×/0.30 numerical aperture objective and 2 × 2
camera binning. CTB-647 imaging used 640 nm excitation and 706 nm emission. Neuronal images
were acquired at 35 positions per device on Plates 1 and 2 and 42 positions per device on Plate 3,
with approximately 10% field overlap.
Image fields were stitched into composite images, aligned to a common brightfield reference, and
cropped to equivalent analysis regions before cell counting. One measurement was obtained per
device. The images were acquired as baseline measurements before axotomy in a separate
experiment. Complete acquisition parameters, image positions, and analytical procedures are
provided in Supplementary Protocol 2.
Statistical analysis - Mold fabrication and repeated casting were summarized descriptively. CTB-
positive cell-body counts were analyzed at the device level and summarized for each plate as the
mean ± standard deviation following exclusion of flagged segmentation artifacts. Because all three
plates contained neurons from a single embryonic preparation, plate-level and device-level
observations were treated as technical replicates rather than independent biological replicates.
Results
OpenMFD enables coordinated design of plate-format microfluidic devices
To link device geometry with the different components required for hybrid mold fabrication, we
developed OpenMFD, an open-source parametric design framework in which shared inputs
determine the photolithographic and three-dimensional (3D) printed components (Fig. 1A). User-
defined parameters include well and channel geometries, compartment spacing, array dimensions,
and alignment features. From these inputs, OpenMFD generates the SU-8 microchannel and SUEX
well/alignment photomasks as Drawing Exchange Format (DXF) files, well-forming insert and
plate-frame models as stereolithography (STL) files, and matching wafer and cutting outlines.
Because the masks and printed inserts are generated from common coordinates, the positions of
insert alignment pins correspond to the openings in the SUEX design. A shared horizontal scaling
factor of 1.0226 was applied to the relevant outputs to account for the anticipated shrinkage of
polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) during curing at 100 °C (Fig. 1A).
For the demonstrated two-compartment neuronal device, the single-unit photomask places two
culture wells on opposite sides of 62 parallel microchannels with a design width of 10 µm and 30
µm interchannel gaps (Fig. 1B). The SU-8 channel features and SUEX well bases and alignment
openings are represented as distinct coordinated mask layers. Repetition of the unit at 18 × 9 mm
spacing produced a wafer-scale layout comprising 48 two-compartment devices in a 6 × 8 array,
with 96 wells on a standard 9 mm plate grid (Fig. 1C). OpenMFD also generated the matching
plate-frame model (Fig. 1D). The corresponding insert models depict the two well-forming

7
structures required for one device and their placement in the complete 96-insert array (Fig. 1E,F).
The assembled microfluidic plate shown in Fig. 1G demonstrates the physical plate format
obtained from this coordinated design.
We next examined whether the same design framework could generate matched files for different
compartment arrangements. OpenMFD produced a four-well, intersecting-channel configuration
inspired by a neuronal–oligodendrocyte myelination assay (PMID: 26015546), including single-
unit and wafer-scale photomasks (Fig. 2A) and corresponding individual and arrayed resin-insert
models (Fig. 2B). A second four-well configuration incorporated orthogonally arranged
connections suitable for an axon-guidance design inspired by gradient-based assays (PMID:
26000554), again yielding matched photomasks (Fig. 2C) and insert models (Fig. 2D). Finally, a
serial three-compartment configuration inspired by a microfluidic synaptic-competition model
(PMID: 24662423) was generated with corresponding photomask (Fig. 2E) and insert outputs (Fig.
2F). OpenMFD generated matched fabrication files for these different compartment numbers and
channel arrangements; the alternative devices were not fabricated, cast or biologically tested.
Integration of photolithography and collectively aligned resin inserts enables fabrication of
reusable hybrid molds
We next implemented the OpenMFD-generated designs by integrating micrometer-scale
photolithographic features with millimeter-scale three-dimensional (3D)-printed resin inserts on
silicon-wafer molds (Fig. 3). The photolithographic structures comprised two nominally 5 µm
SU-8 layers defining the underlying substrate coating and microchannel features, together with a
200 µm SUEX layer defining the well bases and insert-alignment openings. The resulting patterned
wafer accommodated an array of 96 well-forming resin inserts, which were maintained in their
designed relative positions on a detachable metal printing plate before transfer to the wafer (Fig.
3A).
Establishing suitable photolithographic structures required several modifications to the fabrication
procedure. Initial SUEX processing without an LP360 long-pass filter produced raised edges
around patterned features that interfered with the surfaces intended for insert bonding.
Incorporation of the filter visibly reduced these irregularities, providing more uniform contact
surfaces (Supplementary Fig. S1; Supplementary Protocol 1). Adhesion of the SU-8 microchannel
structures was another challenge. Features patterned directly onto silicon detached during
subsequent processing, whereas introducing a continuous, uniformly exposed SU-8 base layer
prevented the observed detachment (Supplementary Fig. S2; Supplementary Protocol 1). Thermal
processing also influenced wafer integrity. Some wafers in an initial batch of eight fabricated
without an additional high-temperature SU-8 bake exhibited warping or layer separation. Both
wafers in a subsequent batch incorporating a 150 °C bake for 10 min remained intact. Although
these observations were obtained from different fabrication batches, they informed the optimized
processing procedure.
A central feature of the hybrid fabrication strategy was the collective alignment of the resin inserts
rather than individual positioning of each well-forming structure. Corresponding alignment
features generated by OpenMFD comprised 1.85 × 1.85 mm square pins on the resin inserts and
2.0 × 2.0 mm openings in the SUEX layer, providing a nominal lateral clearance of 75 µm per side
(Fig. 3B). Maintaining the printed inserts on their detachable build plate preserved their relative

8
positions during transfer, allowing the complete 96-insert array to be positioned against the
patterned wafer in a single operation (Fig. 3A,C).
Simultaneous bonding required accommodation of variation in the heights of the printed inserts.
Measurements across one 96-position array showed a mean pin height of 5.551 mm, a standard
deviation of 26.7 µm, and a total range of 116 µm (5.483–5.599 mm; Supplementary Data File 1,
sheet S1). Rigid clamping did not provide uniform contact across the array. Incorporating a
compressible ethylene propylene diene monomer (EPDM) backing into the clamping assembly
accommodated differences in insert height and enabled collective seating of the alignment pins
within their corresponding SUEX openings (Fig. 3C,D). Following adhesive curing, the flexible
printing plate could be separated from the bonded inserts, leaving the array attached to the
patterned silicon wafer (Fig. 3E). The patterned SUEX features and alignment openings before
insert attachment are shown in Fig. 3F.
The resulting hybrid molds combined lithographically defined microchannels with permanently
attached well-forming inserts. Following deposition of a conformal parylene C coating, the molds
permitted release of cured polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) casts without additional silane-based
release treatment. Microscopic inspection confirmed the presence of open microchannels in the
resulting casts. Together, these findings demonstrate the feasibility of collective insert alignment
and fabrication of reusable hybrid molds incorporating both micrometer- and millimeter-scale
features.
Reusable-mold casting and assembly of a framed PDMS culture plate
The reusable hybrid molds were used to cast complete polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) microfluidic
arrays in which the integrated resin inserts formed the culture wells directly (Fig. 4, steps 1–2).
Each cast contained 48 two-compartment devices with 96 preformed well openings, eliminating
the need to punch individual reservoirs after demolding (Fig. 4, step 5). The well-forming inserts
remained attached to the mold between production cycles, allowing subsequent plates to be cast
without repeating photolithography, insert alignment, or insert bonding. Multiple filled molds
could also be processed in parallel using the same wafer-rack arrangement.
The released PDMS arrays were trimmed along their molded cutting guides and bonded to glass
to produce optically accessible culture substrates (Fig. 4, steps 6–7). Incorporation of the glass-
backed arrays into printed support frames produced complete plate-format devices (Fig. 4, steps
8–9). The final assemblies retained the designed 9 mm well grid and were compatible with standard
plate handling. These steps converted the wafer-scale cast into a practical culture plate while
leaving the microfluidic architecture defined by the reusable mold.
To assess repeated manufacturing performance, we recorded the outcomes of five hybrid molds
assembled using the optimized procedure. Three molds entered routine use and collectively
produced more than 50 usable PDMS casts. Of the two remaining molds, one fractured during
demolding and the other was lost when PDMS leaked beneath the wafer and cured within the wafer
rack. The most recently fabricated molds remained in use for more than eight months without
visible deterioration of their patterned structures or attached inserts. These observations support
repeated mold use, although the available records do not establish a per-cast success rate or mold-
specific lifetime distribution.

9
Assembly of the framed plates required selection of materials compatible with the printing and
culture workflows. High-impact polystyrene (HIPS) exhibited less visible warping than
polypropylene under the frame-printing conditions examined and was selected for subsequent
assemblies. The silicone adhesive LOCTITE SI 5140 was the only tested formulation that
supported primary cortical neuronal cultures through the experimental endpoint. The resulting
frame joints remained visibly intact during routine handling and incubator transfers. These
assessments were qualitative; adhesive cytotoxicity and joint strength were not independently
quantified.
Initial characterization of the finished microchannels was performed using original brightfield
images from one interior device on each of three assembled plates. Nine transverse measurements,
defined by the centers of opposing dark channel-wall bands, corresponded to apparent widths of
10.7–13.1 µm, compared with the nominal 10 µm design width (Supplementary Fig. S3;
Supplementary Data File 1, sheet S4). These image-derived estimates establish the presence of
channels in the cast devices but do not provide a direct measurement of their three-dimensional
cross-sections or depth.
Plate-format handling, directional tracer transport and compartmentalized neuronal
validation
The assembled microfluidic plates retained the standard 9 mm well-centre spacing defined by
OpenMFD, allowing eight wells within a plate column to be filled simultaneously using a
conventional multichannel pipette (Fig. 1G). Both the Opera Phenix Plus and ImageXpress Micro
Confocal high-content imaging systems focused on and acquired images of the assembled arrays
without custom plate handling or instrument modification. The Opera Phenix Plus was used for
the fluorescent tracer and neuronal labeling measurements described below. Thus, the framed
arrays were compatible with established liquid-handling and automated microscopy workflows
without requiring changes to the plate architecture.
We next examined tracer redistribution between the two compartments of 24 devices following
unequal initial loading volumes (Fig. 5A). Alexa Fluor 568-conjugated antibody (red) was
introduced into the left compartment at 25 µL and Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated antibody (green)
into the right compartment at 50 µL. Immediately after loading, fluorescence was predominantly
confined to the respective loading compartments. After 72 h without medium replenishment or
volume adjustment, green fluorescence was visible in the initially lower-volume left
compartments, whereas comparatively little red fluorescence had redistributed in the opposite
direction. The observed pattern was consistent with net tracer transport in the direction of the initial
hydrostatic volume difference. Because fluorescence was recorded only at the initial and final time
points, neither the magnitude nor the persistence of fluid flow could be determined; continuous
compartmental isolation over the 72 h interval was not established.
We then assessed whether the devices supported compartmentalized primary neuronal culture and
retrograde axonal labeling. Cortical neurons isolated from one embryonic day 18 rat embryo were
distributed across three separately assembled plates and maintained for 11 days in vitro (DIV). At
DIV10, Alexa Fluor 647-conjugated cholera toxin subunit B (CTB-647) was applied selectively
to the distal compartments. CTB-positive neuronal cell bodies were observed in the somatic
compartments 24 h later, consistent with axonal extension into the distal compartments, uptake of

10
the tracer, and retrograde transport (Fig. 5B). A representative image from Plate 1, device R03C04,
is shown alongside the corresponding image-analysis outlines used to identify labeled cell bodies.
Long-term neuronal growth was less consistent at the plate perimeter than in the interior devices.
Quantitative analysis was therefore restricted to the 24 interior positions on each of the three plates,
yielding 72 device-level observations. Five counts were excluded from descriptive summaries
because inspection identified segmentation or cell-count artifacts; count magnitude alone was not
an exclusion criterion. The resulting 67 analyzed devices comprised 22, 21, and 24 devices on
Plates 1, 2, and 3, respectively (Fig. 5C; Supplementary Data File 1, sheet S5). Mean CTB-positive
cell-body counts per device were 177.7 ± 43.7 for Plate 1, 269.3 ± 62.3 for Plate 2, and 203.6 ±
32.4 for Plate 3 (mean ± standard deviation). The individual device values and all five excluded
observations are retained in Supplementary Data File 1, sheet S5, and displayed in Fig. 5C. These
were baseline measurements acquired before axotomy in a dimethyl sulfoxide-only experiment.
Because all cultures originated from the same embryo, the plates and devices represent technical
replicates rather than independent biological preparations.
To explore the poorer peripheral culture performance, an additional PDMS array was bonded
directly to glass and cultured without the printed frame or its adhesive in a conventional
polystyrene dish. Peripheral neuronal growth in this configuration appeared comparable to growth
at interior positions, suggesting that the frame, adhesive seal or culture vessel may contribute to
an edge effect.
Taken together, these experiments establish compatibility with plate-based handling and imaging,
demonstrate qualitative tracer redistribution between connected compartments, and support
parallel measurement of retrograde neuronal labeling in interior devices. Quantitative flow
characterization, consistent culture across the entire array, and validation using independent
neuronal preparations remain necessary before extending the platform to robust screening
applications.
Discussion
OpenMFD advances hybrid microfluidic fabrication by integrating coordinated parametric design
with collective resin-insert alignment to produce reusable wafer-scale molds for
compartmentalized culture devices. Previous multiscale fabrication strategies have combined
microscale channels with macroscopic reservoirs using hybrid masters (PMID: 20049640),
integrated lithographically defined microstructures with additively manufactured compartment
walls (PMID: 32832365), and incorporated individually positioned 3D-printed metal inserts into
SU-8 molds (DOI: 10.1088/1361-6439/ab16a7). Building on these approaches, OpenMFD
generates registered photomasks, resin-insert arrays, and supporting plate components from shared
design parameters, enabling the simultaneous alignment and bonding of 96 well-forming inserts
to a patterned silicon wafer. By combining adaptable device design with array-scale mold
assembly and repeated casting, this approach provides a practical manufacturing strategy for
customized medium-throughput microfluidic platforms.
The insert-height measurements (Supplementary Data File 1, sheet S1) identify an important
constraint on collective assembly: across 96 positions, mean pin height was 5.551 mm, with a
standard deviation of 26.7 µm and a 116 µm range. Rigid clamping did not provide uniform

11
contact, whereas a compressible EPDM backing accommodated height variation during bonding.
Square pins and corresponding SUEX openings provided a nominal 75 µm clearance per side,
allowing registration without individual insert positioning. These results support the practicality
of array transfer, but they do not quantify final alignment error or compare bonding yield
statistically between clamping methods. The SU-8 base layer, pre-SUEX bake, and filtered SUEX
exposure likewise reflect process-development solutions to observed adhesion and surface-flatness
problems rather than independently controlled optimization studies.
The retained inserts generated all 96 wells during each PDMS cast, separating one-time
cleanroom-based mold production from routine plate fabrication. Three molds collectively yielded
more than 50 usable casts, and the most recent molds remained in use for over eight months without
visible deterioration. A parylene C coating permitted demolding without additional silane release
treatment and kept the printed resin and adhesive within the mold rather than the finished culture
device. Parylene has previously been investigated as an anti-adhesion coating in PDMS double
casting (DOI: 10.1016/j.sna.2012.09.024). Protective effects of parylene on resin-printed
components have been demonstrated in other biological applications (PMID: 37534979), although
coating performance and potential leaching were not separately quantified here. One wafer
fractured during demolding and another mold was lost after PDMS leaked beneath the wafer; these
distinct failures do not establish a common mechanism. Nor did the present experiments quantify
per-mold casting yields, production time, or cost savings relative to other methods.
The finished microchannels had apparent brightfield widths of 10.7–13.1 µm, compared with the
nominal 10 µm mask design. These nine estimates from three devices (Supplementary Fig. S3;
Supplementary Data File 1, sheet S4) represent preliminary dimensional characterization, not
direct measurements of physical channel cross-sections. Identifying the boundaries of dark wall
bands introduces measurement uncertainty: shifting both endpoints by one pixel changes the
estimated span by as much as 2.37 µm. Channel depth was not measured. The approximately 1 µm
parylene coating is predicted to widen channel-forming ridges by roughly 2 µm, assuming uniform
deposition, but this effect was not isolated experimentally. Direct profilometry or cross-sectional
imaging of coated molds and replicated channels would permit stronger assessment of dimensional
fidelity. Well depth and taper also constrain reservoir volume within the 9 mm spacing; the present
configuration supports up to approximately 50 µL per well.
The framed 48-device arrays accommodated multichannel pipetting and automated imaging on
two high-content microscopy systems without instrument modification. Fluorescent tracer
redistribution was consistent with transport in the direction of an initial hydrostatic volume
difference, but two time points over 72 h could not establish flow rate, pressure stability, or
sustained compartmental isolation. Compartmentalized neuronal cultures have also supported
studies of axon-to-soma signaling and retrograde transport (PMIDs: 34190355; 36826992). In the
present biological demonstration, selective distal application of CTB labeled cortical neuronal
somata (Fig. 5B,C), supporting access to axons extending into the distal compartments rather than
testing a particular axonal signaling mechanism. The 67 analyzed interior devices across three
plates provided a device-level readout, but all neurons originated from one embryo. Thus, these
findings demonstrate assay feasibility and within-preparation variability, not reproducibility across
biological preparations or readiness for screening.
Neuronal growth was less consistent in peripheral devices of framed plates, limiting the number
of positions available for quantitative analysis. Peripheral growth appeared comparable to interior
growth in an unframed PDMS-on-glass array housed in a conventional culture dish, suggesting

12
that the perimeter geometry itself does not preclude culture. Because this comparison altered
frame, adhesive seal, vessel, and surrounding environment together, the underlying cause remains
unresolved. Polypropylene warping is a recognized challenge in filament-based printing (DOI:
10.1002/app.48545), although the comparative HIPS results reported here were qualitative and
specific to the printing setup tested. Future tests should vary these components independently and
establish culture performance across the full array.
Finally, OpenMFD generated coordinated mask and insert files for myelination, orthogonal-
gradient, and serial three-compartment layouts (Fig. 2), extending the design examples beyond the
validated two-compartment plate. Their physical fabrication and biological function remain
untested. Together with complete design files and protocols, these examples provide a basis for
adapting the manufacturing workflow, provided that each new geometry is reassessed for
alignment, demolding, fluid transport, and cell-culture compatibility.
Conclusion  
We developed an open-source fabrication strategy that combines parametric design with collective
alignment of 3D-printed inserts on photolithographically patterned silicon wafers to produce
reusable molds for compartmentalized microfluidic devices. The demonstrated 48-device, 96-well
format enables repeated PDMS casting without individual reservoir punching, with three molds
collectively producing more than 50 usable casts. The assembled plates support conventional
liquid handling, automated imaging, and compartment-specific neuronal assays. By coordinating
design and fabrication across micrometer- and millimeter-scale structures, OpenMFD provides an
adaptable approach for producing customized plate-format microfluidic devices. Further
quantitative characterization of fabrication reproducibility, fluidic performance, and biological
compatibility will establish its suitability for broader experimental applications.
Code and data availability
The OpenMFD source code and fabrication files, including photolithographic masks, three-
dimensional resin-insert models, and plate-frame designs, are available at
https://github.com/trissim/OpenMFD. Supplementary Protocols 1 and 2 describe mold fabrication,
device assembly, culture, and imaging, with Supplementary Figs. S1–S3 documenting
process/device characterization. Supplementary Table S1 compares fabrication approaches; design
dimensions are supplied in Supplementary Data File 1, sheet S6. Supplementary Data File 1
(OpenMFD_Supplementary_Data_File_1.xlsx) contains the 96 resin-insert height measurements
(sheet S1), resin-printing settings (S2), HIPS frame-printing settings (S3), nine apparent
microchannel-width measurements (S4), 72 per-device neuronal cell counts with exclusion flags
(S5), and design specifications (S6). The workbook does not contain the original microscopy
images or native G-code/slicer files, which should be supplied separately with the submission. A
versioned software and fabrication archive will be deposited for permanent access.

Design files
• 
 OpenMFD source and design-generation instructions are available at
https://github.com/trissim/OpenMFD.
•  OpenMFD-generated channel-layer photomask.
•  OpenMFD-generated SUEX well-layer and insert-alignment photomask.
•  OpenMFD-generated resin insert STL array.
•  OpenMFD-generated wafer, cutting, and plate-frame outlines.
Mold and device dimensions
The design specifications in Supplementary Data File 1, sheet S6, describe the experimentally
fabricated two-compartment neuronal layout before parylene coating, except where a measured
property is explicitly indicated.
Materials and equipment
•  6-inch silicon wafer (UniversityWafer ID857).

•  SU-8 2005 negative photoresist (Kayaku Advanced Materials).
•  SUEX K200 dry-film photoresist (DJ MicroLaminates), 200 µm thick.
•  Facility-supplied propylene glycol monomethyl ether acetate (PGMEA), used to develop both
photoresists.
•  LP360 long-pass filter for SUEX exposure.
•  Laurell WS-650-8B spin coater or equivalent.
•  SK 335R6 laminator or equivalent dry-film laminator.
•  EVG620 mask aligner or equivalent photolithography aligner.
•  Elegoo Mars 3 Pro resin printer or locally validated equivalent.
•  Siraya Tech Sculpt Clear high-temperature resin or locally validated equivalent.
•  Detachable magnetic resin-printer build plate or equivalent transfer fixture.
•  Larger bonding plate compatible with the full wafer.
•  Ethylene propylene diene monomer (EPDM) rubber sheet, 0.03125 inch thickness, 60A
durometer.
•  EPO-TEK 301-2 epoxy.
•  Acetone baths and dry air gun.
•  Specialty Coating Systems SCS 200 parylene coater or equivalent parylene C coating service.
A. Generate and verify fabrication files
1. Generate matched photomask, insert, wafer, and frame files from the same OpenMFD preset.
2. Confirm that the channel layer, SUEX well and alignment-hole layer, insert pins, insert skirts,
taper allowances, and cutting/frame outlines share the same coordinate system.
3. To compensate for PDMS shrinkage during curing at 100°C, apply the same horizontal
scale factor of 1.0226 (2.26% enlargement) to the matching mask and insert outputs
(Supplementary Data File 1, sheet S6). Do not add a second scale correction in the
printer’s slicer.
4. Before fabrication, inspect the single-device and wafer-scale DXF outputs and the single and
arrayed insert STL outputs.
B. Pattern and stabilize SU-8/SUEX structures
1. Start with a clean 6-inch silicon wafer. No dehydration bake or hexamethyldisilazane (HMDS)
adhesion-promoter treatment was used in this work.
2. Spin coat SU-8 2005 for a 5 µm target thickness.
3. Flood expose the first SU-8 2005 layer without a mask. Do not develop this layer. This layer
functions as an adhesion base for the microchannel layer.
4. Spin coat a second SU-8 2005 layer for a 5 µm target thickness.
5. Align and expose the second SU-8 layer through the microchannel photomask.

6. Bake and develop the patterned SU-8 layer according to the manufacturer’s SU-8 2005 process
for a 5 µm target thickness.
7. Hard bake the developed two-layer SU-8 stack for 10 min at 150°C before SUEX lamination.
Place the approximately 10 µm stack directly in the heated oven and remove it after 10 min.
No controlled heating or cooling ramp was used for this pre-SUEX bake.
8. Laminate SUEX K200 dry film onto the wafer.
9. Expose the SUEX layer through the well and insert-alignment photomask using an LP360 long-
pass filter at 2800 mJ/cm². The filter blocks shorter-wavelength ultraviolet light.
10. Post-exposure bake by ramping from room temperature to 50°C at 1°C/min, holding at 50°C
for at least 12 h overnight, then shutting off the oven and allowing it to cool.
11. Develop the SUEX layer in PGMEA for 20 min with mixing, exchanging developer at 15 min.
12. Hard bake by ramping from room temperature to 120°C at 3°C/min, holding for 30 min, and
ramping down by powering off the oven.
13. Check that the microchannels remain attached, the SUEX features and alignment holes are
intact, and the SUEX surfaces are flat enough for a continuous epoxy seal.
Troubleshooting note — SUEX surface flatness.  Exposure without the LP360 long-pass filter
produced raised edges around SUEX features that interfered with the epoxy bonding surface.
LP360-filtered exposure markedly reduced the raised edges (Supplementary Fig. S1). Check that
the SUEX surface allows a continuous insert–wafer seal before bonding.
Supplementary Fig. S1. SUEX K200 well-base features following exposure without (left) and
with (right) an LP360 long-pass filter. Edge ridges are evident in the unfiltered example and
substantially reduced in the filtered example. Qualitative development comparison.

Troubleshooting note — SU-8 adhesion and thermal stability.  If SU-8 is patterned directly on
bare silicon without the continuous flood-exposed base layer, channel structures may delaminate
(Supplementary Fig. S2). The 150 °C, 10 min pre-SUEX bake is also important: partial layer
warping/separation was observed in a development batch of eight wafers in which that bake was
omitted, whereas two wafers subsequently processed with the bake remained intact. These are
process-development observations, not a controlled comparison.
Supplementary Fig. S2. Examples of delaminated SU-8 microchannel structures after patterning
directly on bare silicon without the flood-exposed base. Scale bars in the original micrographs:
100 µm (left) and 200 µm (right).
C. Print, clean and inspect the resin-insert array
1. Print the OpenMFD-generated insert array. This work used Siraya Tech Sculpt Clear resin on
an Elegoo Mars 3 Pro printer with the settings supplied in the original resin-printer profile.
Test settings for other printers and resins before printing the full array.
2. Record resin, layer height, exposure, lift/retract, washing, and post-cure settings with the local
printer profile. These settings apply to the local printer and resin, independently of the device
dimensions in OpenMFD.
3. Clean the printed inserts by spraying with acetone and blow drying with compressed nitrogen.
Repeat until pin features are free of residual resin; this work used 6–8 acetone/nitrogen cycles.
4. Remove the flexible metal build plate from the printer platform and post-cure the print in an
Elegoo Mercury X rotating UV cure station for 15 min.
5. Keep the inserts in their printed relative positions on the detachable flexible metal build plate or
equivalent transfer fixture.
6. Inspect all insert pins and the printed array. Pin-height measurements on one 8 × 12 array
showed a 116 µm range and were used to select the compressible backing; measurement of
every production array is not required for the reported procedure (Supplementary Data File 1,
sheet S1). The resin exposure, lift/retract, wash and post-cure settings are summarized in
Supplementary Data File 1, sheet S2; retain the native profile with the associated slicer profile.
7. Before bonding, verify that inserts remain attached to the flexible transfer plate in their printed
relative positions and that no resin obstructs the alignment pins.

D. Align and bond all inserts to the patterned wafer
1. Move the flexible metal build plate carrying the insert array to a bonding plate suitable for
clamping against the full wafer. Keep the inserts on the flexible plate in their printed relative
positions.
2. Place a 0.03125-inch-thick, 60A EPDM rubber sheet between the fixed magnet on the clamping
build plate and the flexible metal build plate carrying the inserts.
3. Apply EPO-TEK 301-2 epoxy in excess to the underside cavity on the pin side of each insert.
4. Place the wafer with SU-8/SUEX features facing the insert pins.
5. Align the wafer until all insert pins seat into their corresponding SUEX alignment holes.
6. Place a second flat plate above the wafer and clamp the stack to spread epoxy at the insert-wafer
interface.
7. Submerge the clamped assembly in acetone for 1 min.
8. Transfer to a fresh acetone bath for a second 1 min wash.
9. Blow-dry the assembly thoroughly with dry air until the joints and nearby mold features are as
dry and visibly clear as possible.
10. Cure the clamped assembly at room temperature for 48 h.
11. After cure, sonicate the bonded insert-wafer assembly in acetone for 10 min to remove residual
material.
12. Release the bonded insert array from the transfer fixture by flexing the flexible metal build
plate while preserving the insert-wafer bond.
13. After release, check that the wafer is intact and that all inserts remain bonded with their pins
seated in the alignment holes.
E. Apply parylene C and qualify the mold
1. Coat the bonded hybrid mold with 1 µm parylene C.
2. This work used a Specialty Coating Systems SCS 200 coater. Use a local parylene coater or
send the completed hybrid mold to an external university core or commercial coating service.
3. After coating, store and handle the mold as a reusable wafer-scale mold for PDMS casting.
4. Inspect the first PDMS cast for clean release, open wells, and intact channel regions. The
design dimensions in Supplementary Data File 1, sheet S6, refer to the mold before
coating.
Acceptance criterion: the completed mold remains intact, the inserts remain bonded, and the first
cast releases with open well reservoirs and continuous microchannel regions. Evaluate each mold
after subsequent casting cycles. Aggregate mold-use results are reported in the manuscript
Results, not as steps of this protocol.

Supplementary Protocol 2. Post-mold device assembly, primary cortical neuron culture, and
CTB retrograde axon tracing
Purpose and scope
Cast PDMS from the mold prepared in Supplementary Protocol 1; trim, glass-bond and frame the
plate; assess fluorescent-solution redistribution; and culture embryonic cortical neurons for
retrograde tracing using Alexa Fluor 647–conjugated cholera toxin subunit B (CTB-647). The 48-
device plate contains 96 wells on a standard 9 mm well grid, with a maximum working volume of
50 µL per well. Primary culture measurements were restricted to 24 interior devices per plate
because growth was poorer at the perimeter.
Materials and equipment
•  Completed parylene-coated hybrid mold (Supplementary Protocol 1).
•  Sylgard 184 PDMS base and curing agent.
•  60 mL syringe for dispensing PDMS into the wafer mold.
•  Vacuum desiccator and 100°C oven.
•  Industrial paper guillotine and clean razor blades.
•  Coverslip glass, 110 × 74 × 0.17 mm.
•  Harrick PDC-001 plasma cleaner or equivalent.
•  Dry-air supply for plasma treatment.
•  Sterilization pouches and autoclave operated at 121°C for 15 min.
•  OpenMFD-generated HIPS frame printed on an enclosed FDM printer.
•  12-channel pipette fitted with eight tips.
•  70% ethanol.
•  Henkel LOCTITE SI 5140 one-part alkoxy-cure RTV silicone sealant (3 oz tube, IDH 135264),
3 mL Luer-lock syringe, and 18 gauge dispensing needle.
•  Dendritic polyglycerol amine (dPGA; DendroTEK Biosciences) surface-coating reagent.
•  DMEM with 10% fetal bovine serum.
•  Neurobasal Plus medium supplemented with 1% N2, 2% B27, and 1% glutamine.
•  Primary E18 Sprague Dawley rat cortical neurons.
•  Alexa Fluor-conjugated cholera toxin subunit B (CTB-647).
•  Alexa Fluor 488- and Alexa Fluor 568-conjugated secondary antibodies.
•  PerkinElmer Opera Phenix Plus high-content imaging system with a 10×/0.30 NA objective.
A. Cast and demold PDMS devices
1. Form a leak-tight aluminum-foil reservoir around the parylene-coated wafer mold.
2. Mix Sylgard 184 at a 10:1 base:curing-agent ratio. Approximately 35 mL total mixture is
sufficient for one wafer mold.

3. Transfer approximately 30 mL of the mixed PDMS into a 60 mL syringe, then dispense it
over the mold, stopping below the insert tops to leave the wells open.
4. Load the filled molds into the six-shelf metal wafer rack and place the rack in the cylindrical
vacuum chamber. Degas until visible bubbles are removed (typically 10–30 min;
approximately −15 inHg in this setup).
5. Transfer the loaded rack to the oven. Cure for 1 h at 100°C and allow the mold to return to
room temperature.
6. Remove the aluminum foil and release the PDMS around the mold perimeter.
7. Support the wafer on a flat surface. Start peeling at the corners and progress toward the center
while pulling the PDMS upward and backward to reduce stress on the wafer.
8. Inspect the demolded cast. Wells must be open, microchannel regions must be intact, and no
insert or SU-8/SUEX feature may have detached from the mold.
B. Trim and bond PDMS to glass
1. Place the demolded PDMS feature-side up on a clean sheet of paper on the industrial paper-
guillotine bed.
2. Apply clean low-residue tape along the inner edge of each molded cutting wall. Overlap the
wall and extend each strip beyond the circular cast onto the paper so that the cast is held flat.
Align the molded cutting guide with the guillotine blade.
3. Trim the device to the generated 108 × 72 mm outline and cut a small 45° chamfer at each corner
for frame alignment.
4. Remove particles from the bonding surface with repeated application of clean tape. Keep the
final protective layer in place until plasma treatment.
5. Place the PDMS and a clean 110 × 74 × 0.17 mm coverslip-glass sheet in the plasma cleaner
with the bonding surfaces exposed.
6. Treat with dry-air plasma for 1 min at 200–600 mTorr in a Harrick PDC-001, or use locally
validated equivalent conditions, to activate both surfaces for PDMS-glass bonding.
7. Bring the activated surfaces into contact while maintaining a uniform glass margin around the
PDMS. Apply gentle pressure from the center outward.
8. Heat the bonded assembly at 100°C for at least 1 min while applying uniform pressure.
9. Check that the PDMS and glass are sealed, then autoclave the bonded assembly in a sterilization
pouch at 121°C for 15 min.
C. Assemble and condition the framed plate
1. Decontaminate the HIPS frame with 70% ethanol, allow it to dry, and invert it so that the
adhesive groove surrounding the device opening faces upward.
2. Dispense 0.5–1 mL LOCTITE SI 5140 into the upward-facing frame groove using an 18 gauge
dispensing needle.
3. Invert the bonded PDMS-on-glass assembly so that the glass faces upward. Align the PDMS
with the frame recess and lower the assembly into the frame.

4. Inspect the adhesive joint for visible gaps.
5. Cure at room temperature for 3 days, turn the framed device upright, and trim excess cured
adhesive with a clean razor blade.
6. Before coating or culture, plasma-treat the assembled device in a Harrick PDC-001 with dry air
at high power (30 W) for 10 min at approximately 400 mTorr to decontaminate the surface
and make it hydrophilic. Begin aqueous coating within 15 min of plasma treatment.
Important distinction.  The first plasma treatment activates PDMS and glass for bonding (section
B); the second treatment prepares the assembled plate for aqueous coating and culture (section C).
The reported experiments used LOCTITE SI 5140: alternative frame adhesives require
independent validation for cell survival, bond integrity and leakage.
D. Compare fluorescent-solution redistribution between compartments
Imaging settings used in sections D and F: widefield acquisition on a PerkinElmer Opera Phenix
Plus with 10×/0.30 NA objective, 2 × 2 camera binning and 100 ms fluorescence exposures. The
effective pixel size was 1.187 µm. Apply appropriate green and red detection channels for this
assay; retain identical settings across samples within each assay.
1. Reserve 24 assembled two-compartment devices for the directional fluid movement assay.
2. Prepare Alexa Fluor 488- and Alexa Fluor 568-conjugated secondary antibodies, each at a
1:1000 dilution in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS).
3. Add 25 µL Alexa Fluor 568 solution to the left compartment of each device.
4. Add 50 µL Alexa Fluor 488 solution to the right compartment.
5. Image the complete device set immediately after loading (Hour 0) using the shared fluorescence-
imaging settings above.
6. Keep the devices in a cell-culture incubator for 72 h without replenishing either compartment
or adjusting the volumes, then image the same devices.
7. Compare green fluorescence in the initially lower-volume left compartment and red
fluorescence in the right compartment between Hour 0 and 72 h.
Interpretation: this qualitative experiment describes redistribution between wells under the tested
volume imbalance; it does not independently establish the kinetics of flow or long-term fluidic
isolation.
E. Coat and culture primary cortical neurons
1. Isolate cortical neurons from one embryonic day 18 (E18) Sprague Dawley rat embryo following
an established neuronal compartmentalization protocol (PMID: 18989412).
2. Distribute neurons from that embryo across three separately assembled plates. Because the
neurons all come from the same embryo, the plates are technical replicates, not independent
biological samples.
3. Add 30 µL of 10 µg/mL dPGA to each culture well, incubate for 10 min, and wash once with
sterile water. dPGA was selected as the neuronal culture substrate based on published work
on dendritic polyglycerol amine (PMID: 35023760).
4. Add 50 µL supplemented Neurobasal Plus medium to the distal compartment.

5. Seed 5,000–10,000 neurons in 50 µL DMEM with 10% fetal bovine serum in the cell-body
(soma) compartment.
6. Allow cells to attach for at least 30 min, then replace the soma-compartment medium with 50
µL supplemented Neurobasal Plus medium.
7. Remove 25 µL from the distal compartment. Maintain 50 µL in the soma compartment and 25
µL in the distal compartment to create a small pressure difference that directs fluid from the
soma compartment toward the distal compartment.
8. Maintain cultures for 11 days in vitro (DIV11) following the established compartmentalized
neuronal culture procedure (PMID: 18989412), with the medium formulation and
compartment volumes specified above applied across all three plates.
F. Perform distal CTB labeling and image acquisition
1. To check whether cultured neurons have extended axons into the distal compartment, apply
CTB there and image labeled cell bodies in the soma compartment 24 h later. Axons take up
CTB in the distal compartment and transport it back to their cell bodies.
2. At DIV10, add CTB-647 to the 25 µL distal compartment at a final concentration of 1 µg/mL.
3. After adding CTB, keep 50 µL in the soma compartment and 25 µL in the distal compartment.
4. Incubate for 24 h.
5. At DIV11, collect brightfield and Alexa 647 images using the shared fluorescence-imaging
settings above.
6. Collect overlapping images and stitch them into one image per device. In this experiment, Plates
1 and 2 used 35 imaging positions per device (7 × 5 grid), and Plate 3 used 42 positions (7 ×
6 grid), with approximately 10% overlap.
7. Align each stitched brightfield image to the reference brightfield image and crop all plates to
the same area for cell counting, regardless of whether images were collected at 35 or 42
positions. Imaging a larger area does not enlarge the area used for counting.
8. Identify and count CTB-positive neuronal cell bodies using the same cell segmentation settings
and criteria for CTB labeling in every cropped image. Record one CTB-positive cell-body
count for each cropped device.
For CTB imaging, use laser autofocus, 640 nm excitation and 706 nm emission for Alexa 647, and
a 10 ms brightfield exposure. Plate 3 required a larger acquisition grid because of a slight shift of
the PDMS array during frame assembly; after alignment, all plates were cropped to the same
counting region.
G. Cell counting and analysis set
1. Inspect the stitched images and segmentation overlays; verify that selected objects represent
CTB-positive neuronal cell bodies rather than background or other segmentation artifacts.
2. Apply the same segmentation settings and counting region to each device, including the plates
collected using different acquisition grids.
3. For the February 2026 DMSO-only experiment, examine the 24 interior devices of each of three
plates (72 images total). Exclude only the five images with identified segmentation/counting

artifacts (two from Plate 1, three from Plate 2), leaving n = 22, 21 and 24 devices for Plates
1–3, respectively.
4. Report per-plate counts as mean ± sample standard deviation across the included devices. Do
not exclude observations solely because counts are unusually high or low. The three plates
received neurons from a single E18 rat embryo; their counts describe technical variation, not
variation between independent biological preparations.
H. Optional post-cast measurement of apparent microchannel width
This characterization supports the manuscript microchannel-width results; it is not a required
routine casting step. For device R02C02 from each of three plates, three brightfield channel spans
were measured from the centres of opposing dark wall bands using the native image calibration
(1.18675253 µm per pixel). The nine measured spans were 9–11 pixels, corresponding to apparent
widths of 10.7–13.1 µm. Moving both chosen endpoints by one pixel can change the measurement
by up to 2.37 µm. The relationship between the optical dark bands and the physical channel walls
was not established, and neither channel depth nor the complete cross-section was measured. The
recorded values and pixel coordinates are tabulated in Supplementary Data File 1, sheet S4.
